pages.title: Languages of Odisha
pages.lead: Begin with a language you know, or one you want to understand. Follow its writing, books and speakers—and notice where a familiar name can mean something different.

paragraphs.text: Kui and Kuvi have separate entries in SCSTRTI’s catalogue of trilingual learning booklets. The same catalogue offers resources labelled Santali, Saora, Ho, Juang and Koya. These publications give you something specific to begin with: a named learning resource, rather than a general description of a community.

Follow each title into its own introduction. A similar spelling is a reason to look more closely, not to merge two names. A teaching booklet is also only one view of a language; it cannot stand for every speaker, locality or kind of writing.

Santali and Ol Chiki show why the distinction matters. The President’s Secretariat’s account of the 2026 Ol Chiki celebration credits Raghunath Murmu with creating the script in 1925. It also describes earlier use of Roman, Devanagari, Odia and Bengali scripts for Santali.

A date in the history of a script is not a birth date for the language. Nor does a script name tell you everything about the literature written in it. The Santali introduction follows the writing into named books and literary gatherings; the small specimen in this directory spells “Ol Chiki”, the script’s name.

When someone shares a word or expression, ask what they call their language, where they use it and who taught it to them. Keep that context with the example. A family’s name for its speech, a publication’s title and an administrative label may answer different questions.

Odia is the starting point for this collection, with other languages receiving their own introductions. The Sambalpuri page considers the names Sambalpuri and Kosali without treating their preferred use as settled for every speaker. The Desia page follows learning and theatre projects. These are paths to explore, not a complete inventory of Odisha’s languages.

pages.title: Odia
pages.lead: A palm-leaf manuscript, a girl learning to read, a book for newcomers: three ways to begin exploring Odia, through the things people write, hear and learn.

paragraphs.text: A cord holds the palm leaves together; beside them lies a metal writing stylus, or lekhani. Prateek Pattanaik photographed this Odia manuscript at Gyana Mandira library in Koraput. The photograph lets us see the object’s shape and binding, though it does not identify the text or date the manuscript.

A manuscript gives a written work a physical form. To understand its history, we would also want to know who copied it, when, and from which earlier text. The age of a surviving copy and the age of the language are different questions.

sections.title: Writing made for more than the page

paragraphs.text: In his literary overview, Ganeswar Mishra places Sarala Das’s Mahabharata in the fifteenth century. He describes a medieval poetic world of narratives, devotional poems and varied verse forms, with performers helping works reach audiences. Reading this history only as a succession of books would miss the part played by people voicing them.

That connection between a written work and a listening audience becomes easier to see in a particular story. A list of literary names tells us where to begin; a scene can show what people do with words.

In Fakir Mohan Senapati’s story Rebati, the girl sits beside her father as he sings devotional songs and sometimes reads the Bhagabata. She learns songs by listening. Later, the teacher Basudev brings her a primer containing pictures of elephants, horses and cattle, and begins teaching her letters. Her father supports her learning; her grandmother objects, insisting that a girl should learn domestic work instead.

The story brings two kinds of learning into the same household: remembering a song and learning to read a page. It also makes access to education a family argument. These are details of Senapati’s fiction, not evidence that every Odia household lived in the same way. They offer a specific question to carry into the story: who is encouraged to learn, and who is held back?

For a structured introduction, CIIL’s catalogue lists Odia Language, Literature and Culture: An Introduction, edited by Sanjaya Kumar Bag and issued in 2019. Its stated audience is non-native learners, and its recorded language is Odia. A book’s intended audience and the language in which it teaches are both worth checking before choosing it.

If you are beginning from spoken Odia, try reading a short passage with someone who can explain unfamiliar words. If you are beginning through English, keep the translator and edition beside the title. Hearing a passage, reading it in Odia and reading a translation offer different ways into the same work; none needs to stand for the whole language.

The linked population atlas answers another question: how people’s mother tongues were recorded in a particular census. It does not tell us which books they read, how they spoke at home, or how many languages they used.

pages.title: Santali
pages.lead: Santali has more than one written life. Ol Chiki offers a way to follow its sounds into books, classrooms and literary conversation.

paragraphs.text: Santali is the language; Ol Chiki is one of the scripts used to write it. The President’s Secretariat dates Raghunath Murmu’s creation of Ol Chiki to 1925. Its account of the centenary gathering held in New Delhi on 16 February 2026 also recalls Santali being written in Roman, Devanagari, Odia and Bengali scripts. The new alphabet belongs within that longer writing history.

A script’s anniversary does not date the beginning of a language. Nor does celebrating Ol Chiki tell us which script every reader uses. When opening a Santali book, notice the writing on the page as well as the language named on the cover: they answer different questions.

Ol Chiki runs from left to right. Its vowels are written as letters of their own, rather than being built into a consonant and altered around it. That makes it an alphabet, structurally different from the neighbouring Indic writing systems described as abugidas. Recognising a letter’s outline is therefore only a beginning; the reader also learns how letters represent the sounds of Santali.

Small marks matter. A raised dot marks a nasalized vowel, while a separate length mark can follow an oral or nasalized vowel. Unicode’s description also distinguishes a dot at the baseline that modifies certain vowels. These are parts of the writing system, not decorative details. A fluent reader can help a learner hear the differences that the marks preserve.

A particular book gives the reader somewhere to begin. Nalha, a poetry collection by Gobinda Chandra Majhi, appears as the 2016 winner in Sahitya Akademi’s Santali award register. That identifies a work to seek out; it does not supply the book’s publication date, an English translation or an account of what its poems say. Begin with an edition, and keep the author and any translator visible as you read.

Literary life also takes place around the books. At a symposium in Baripada on 21 May 2022, organised by Sahitya Akademi with the Santali department of MSCBD University, Damayanti Beshra chaired the inaugural session and spoke about the language’s present situation. The report records separate presentations on movements for Santali language, script and literature in Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal. It shows writers and scholars examining regional histories together, rather than treating a script’s invention as the end of the story.

The Santali learning booklet published by the Special Development Council, Mayurbhanj, places English, Odia and Santali alongside one another. Its first-edition credits name November 2018 and the compilers Mangat Murmu, Raghunath Hembram and Saluram Hembram. This is one dated teaching resource, with named people behind it; it need not stand for every locality’s words or every reader’s preferred spelling.

Use the linked booklet as a shared page, not a substitute for listening. Ask a willing reader which forms they use, what a printed example leaves unexplained and which book they would recommend next. An answer may lead to a poem, a different script or a local expression. Keep that person’s chosen credit with anything they permit you to share.

pages.title: Odia Literature
pages.lead: A narrator who makes praise sound suspicious. An epic character who questions her own journey. Begin with a passage, and listen to who is telling it.

paragraphs.text: The opening of Fakir Mohan Senapati’s Chha Mana Atha Guntha, known in English as Six Acres and a Third, introduces Ramachandra Mangaraj as a devout man. Then a servant mentions food set aside in his house on fasting evenings and empty vessels the next morning. The narrator rushes to his defence: nobody saw him eat; liquids can evaporate; animals might have taken the food.

The defence is so elaborate that it invites suspicion. We hear the praise, notice the excuses and begin judging for ourselves. Before following the struggle over land, there is already something to listen for: the distance between what this narrator says and what the reader is encouraged to think.

In the English excerpt of Jajnaseni on Pratibha Ray’s website, Draupadi thinks about attachment while travelling towards heaven through the Himalayas. She wonders whether even this desire has become a kind of bondage. When she falls, her five husbands continue without looking back. The passage gives us the journey through her thoughts and the abandonment she describes.

Compare that voice with Senapati’s narrator. One draws us into a public performance of praise and excuse; the other lets us hear a character question the meaning of her own life. Who gets to speak changes what we notice. These two openings into a work offer a way to choose your next reading without reducing a whole literary tradition to a list of famous names.

sections.title: Keep the translator beside the title

paragraphs.text: The University of California Press paperback of Six Acres and a Third lists four translators: Rabi Shankar Mishra, Satya Mohanty, Jatindra N. Nayak and Paul St.-Pierre. Its December 2005 publication date belongs to that English edition. It is not the date when Senapati wrote the Odia novel.

An English title alone may not tell you which translation you have. Keep the translator, publisher and edition with your reading notes. If you can read both languages, try comparing a short exchange: where does the joke land, how does a character address another person, and which words need explanation? If you are reading only in translation, an introduction or translator’s note can help you understand those choices.

Choose a writer or work below, then read a scene slowly. Mark one sentence that changed your impression of a character. Return to it after the next chapter. You do not need to settle the meaning of the whole book before noticing how it works.

The introductions here are starting points. Follow their sources to a text or an identified edition, and let a particular poem, story or novel lead the way. Biography can add context; the words on the page still deserve your attention.

pages.title: Fakir Mohan Senapati
pages.kicker: Literary lives · Odia language and Odisha
pages.lead: A girl turns the pages of her first primer. A narrator makes an educated reader explain what he knows about his neighbours. Fakir Mohan Senapati’s stories ask who gets to learn, who gets heard and whose knowledge counts.

paragraphs.text: Fakir Mohan Senapati (1843–1918) was born at Malikashapur near Balasore. Orphaned young, he grew up with his grandmother and had limited formal schooling. His working life included teaching and service as a dewan, an administrative officer in princely states.

These different kinds of work offer useful context for reading him. A classroom, an account book and a household all involve authority: someone decides what is worth learning, what is owed and whose explanation will be believed. His fiction lets us watch such decisions at close quarters.

sections.title: Making room for Odia in print

paragraphs.text: Odia’s place in school education was being challenged during Senapati’s lifetime. Geetashree Priyambada’s historical account connects his textbook writing with opposition to proposals to remove Odia from schools. A language needed books as well as arguments in its defence.

Ramakanta Rout records that Senapati brought a printing press from Calcutta to Balasore in 1868, published Sambada Bahika and Bodhadayini, organised public meetings and wrote in Utkal Dipika. The account places him alongside other participants in the language movement.

Textbooks gave pupils something to read; a press made more copies possible; journals carried arguments beyond a single classroom. Read together, these activities show how defending a language could involve the practical work of writing, printing and circulation.

sections.title: Language and the making of Odisha

paragraphs.text: Odia-speaking regions were divided among several administrations. Priyambada places the movement for their unification, Desha Mishran Andolan, alongside the effort to strengthen Odia language and literature. These were connected concerns, with many participants and a history longer than one writer’s life.

Odisha became a separate province on 1 April 1936, eighteen years after Senapati’s death. His educational and literary work belongs to the earlier foundations of that movement; the later province was a collective achievement.

In Rebati, a girl learns devotional songs by listening to her father before she begins lessons with Basudev. When he brings an illustrated primer, she turns its pages and shows the animal pictures to her mother and grandmother. Her grandmother wants her to learn cooking and household work instead. The wish to read is already part of a family conversation.

The story later sets two explanations beside each other. After her parents die in an epidemic, the landlord’s men take the family’s cows for alleged arrears and withdraw its cultivation land. The grandmother blames Rebati’s education for their disasters. Yet the narrative has shown illness, lost income and dispossession. Her accusation asks us to notice whom grief makes responsible, and what that blame leaves out.

sections.title: The narrator turns towards the reader

paragraphs.text: Chha Mana Atha Guntha, known in English as Six Acres and a Third, introduces the landlord and moneylender Ramachandra Mangaraj through his reputation for piety. Details about food disappearing on fasting days unsettle the narrator’s elaborate defence of him. Praise becomes a way of making the reader suspicious.

Chapter 10 turns the joke towards educated readers. Its narrator mocks men who can recite foreign genealogies but know little about their own neighbours. He explains the weavers’ community fund and then describes a village temple as a place of worship, public reading, meals and collective deliberation. To make those functions intelligible to his audience, he reaches for English labels: church, public library, hotel and town hall.

The comparison reverses an expectation. A familiar village institution must apparently acquire English names before an educated reader can recognise its uses. The passage is an argument made by a fictional narrator, with its own defence of community authority. It invites attention to local knowledge without supplying a neutral survey of every village.

sections.title: Patent Medicine: laughter with an uncomfortable ending

paragraphs.text: In Patent Medicine, Chandramani tries to escape his wife Sulochana’s restrictions on his outings. He invents a religious observance, persuades the servant Makara to lie under a covering in his place and goes out. When he returns intoxicated, Sulochana beats him with a broom; later she sees his injuries, regrets what she has done and tends him.

In the closing exchange, Gopi Babu jokingly calls the beating a new remedy for his conduct. The story also describes the couple’s quieter life, reading Utkal Sahitya, Mukur and Dipika together. The movement from deception to violence, remorse and care makes an uneasy comedy. Read the wife’s authority alongside the demands of wifely devotion, and keep the injury in view when the narrator invites laughter.

sections.title: Listen for a change in tone

paragraphs.text: Set these passages beside one another. In the novel, the narrator keeps addressing an audience and testing its assumptions. In Rebati, a child’s enthusiasm gives way to isolation. Patent Medicine makes the reader negotiate a joke whose consequences have hurt someone. Rather than deciding in advance that Senapati is simply humorous or realistic, notice how each story directs your sympathy.
His other writing includes the novels Mamu, Lachhama and Prayaschitta, poetry, and the autobiography Atma Jibana Charita. These offer further reading beyond the stories discussed here.

An autobiography adds a different kind of voice: a writer remembers and arranges his own life. Keep those memories beside a chronology rather than treating literary recollection as an independent record of every event.

Begin with Rebati and follow what changes between the first primer and the household’s losses. Read Patent Medicine next, paying attention to the ending as well as the trick. Then enter Chha Mana Atha Guntha through its narrator, continuing beyond the opening chapters before deciding what the whole novel argues.

A book can be a starting point for exploring Balasore’s literary connections. Ask a local bookseller which edition readers return to. Keep the documented places in Senapati’s life separate from the imagined geography of his fiction, and check memorial access or opening hours locally before planning a visit.

pages.title: Six Acres and a Third
pages.lead: A cow can be a daughter to one household and a source of milk to a man discussing its yield. In Fakir Mohan Senapati’s novel, such differences in how people value things help explain why a small holding matters.

paragraphs.text: Chha Mana Atha Guntha, known in English as Six Acres and a Third, is a novel by Fakir Mohan Senapati. In the chapter introducing Bhagia and Saria, the couple work together: she helps with his weaving, and he tends the fire and brings water while she cooks. Their cow, Neta, is treated as a daughter. The narrator counts her as a third member of the household.

The same chapter gives the land a history. Bhagia’s father bought the fertile, rent-free holding; Bhagia receives a share of its grain while someone else cultivates it. He is a weaver with an inherited source of support. The narrator sets this household security beside Mangaraj’s interested reaction to the cow’s milk yield. What Saria loves as family can also be appraised as an asset.

sections.title: How a defence becomes an accusation

paragraphs.text: The opening chapter introduces Ramachandra Mangaraj as a landlord and moneylender with a reputation for religious observance. The narrator seems eager to protect that reputation. Yet the account of his fasting includes food disappearing at night, followed by an elaborate defence. The details make the praise difficult to accept at face value.

This is a useful way into the novel’s humour: listen to what the narrator claims, then look at the evidence he has just supplied. His apparent loyalty to a respectable man can give the reader reasons to distrust that man. The joke asks us to do some of the judging.

sections.title: The reader is also under examination

paragraphs.text: In Bhagia and Saria’s chapter, the narrator anticipates a reader’s contempt for the weavers’ hereditary leadership. He then turns to inherited religious authority among the reader’s own people. The criticism changes direction. Customs dismissed as foolish in one community look less easy to dismiss when their logic appears closer to home.

His interruptions matter. He addresses the reader, imagines objections and moves between an account of village life and an argument about the person reading it. Following the plot therefore also means asking what assumptions the narrator has caught us making.

sections.title: Who gets heard in the courtroom?

paragraphs.text: The opening of the Cuttack Sessions Court chapter places Mangaraj before a crowded court. In the narrator’s satirical account, the judge ordinarily leaves much of the work to a subordinate while reading or writing letters. Today an English witness requires his own attention, and the judgment must be written in English.

Then the narrator pauses: he and his readers are Odia, and the printing letters are local, so he must translate the proceedings. The aside makes language part of the scene’s unequal authority. It also reminds us that the court reaches us through a storyteller who chooses how to present it. This is a fictional scene, not a record of an actual trial.

paragraphs.text: The University of California Press paperback dates from December 2005, ISBN 9780520228832. Its listing credits Rabi Shankar Mishra, Satya Mohanty, Jatindra N. Nayak and Paul St.-Pierre as translators. Those are the publisher’s display names; the date identifies this English edition.

The original Odia publication chronology remains open in the project’s evidence. Peter Samuels’s teaching essay gives 1902; Ramakanta Rout’s historical account gives 1905. pages.title: Kui
pages.lead: A learning page brings pictures, letters and a reader’s voice together. Follow Kui into the books and the people who prepare them.

paragraphs.text: Kui belongs to the South-Central Dravidian language family. CIIL describes it as closely related to Kuvi and Gondi, but related names do not make these languages interchangeable. A Kui learning page and a Kuvi learning page belong to different introductions; begin with the language the reader actually uses.

sections.title: From a picture to a written mark

paragraphs.text: The CIIL–NCERT Kui Primer, first published on 9 March 2024, introduces letters and basic numerals for young children and adult literacy. On printed page 3, a mouse photograph accompanies a large letter, word labels and progressively lighter letter forms for tracing. The page joins recognising a pictured object with recognising and making a written mark.

Later, a counting page aligns numerals and word labels with increasing rows of fruit pictures. A reader can follow the quantity visually before comparing its written forms. These are particular choices made for a learning book, rather than a complete account of how anyone speaks Kui.

The development credits connect the book to Kandhamal: teacher Bapuji Pradhan in Daringbadi, teacher Udhaba Kanhar in Balliguda, Kui author Srikant Mallick and teacher educator Anita Kumari Mallick in Tikabali are among its resource persons. Anuj Mohan Pradhan is listed as a reviewer.

There is also a literary reading lead. ATLC’s catalogue lists Tahii, a Kui short-story collection by Anuj Mohan Pradhan, dated 2015. That gives a reader a named work to seek alongside teaching materials. The catalogue identifies the collection; it does not tell us how its stories unfold.

When you find an edition, begin with one story and a willing reader. Ask who speaks, what the opening asks you to notice, and how a passage sounds when read aloud. Let the actual writing lead the conversation before asking it to represent an entire community.

An earlier learning resource offers a different arrangement: the November 2018 Kui booklet places English, Odia and Kui side by side. Published by the Special Development Council, Kandhamal, it credits Susil Kumar Digal and Ranjit Kumar Pradhan as compilers. A comparison page makes those relationships visible.

Choose an entry together, then ask for a sentence in which the reader would use it. Keep the printed example and their explanation distinct. A table offers a starting point; the conversation can reveal local usage, context and the difference between recognising a word and knowing when to say it.

pages.lead: Follow Kuvi from spoken words into a picture lesson, a comparison booklet and a collection of tales, songs and riddles.

sections.title: A language, not a spelling variation

paragraphs.text: Kuvi is a Dravidian language spoken in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. Its use of Odia letters does not make it Odia, and the similar-looking name Kui belongs to a related language with its own learning materials. Start with the language named by the speaker or book, rather than guessing from the script.

The census figure below has a narrower meaning than the language’s reach. It records the individual Kuvi mother-tongue return in Odisha in 2011. It is neither a present-day count nor a total for everyone who speaks Kuvi across state borders.

sections.title: Putting a spoken repertoire on the page

paragraphs.text: Kuvi Folk Literature offers one route from speech into print. CIIL’s catalogue describes a collection of twelve tales, twenty songs and thirty-five riddles, transcribed in a modified Odia script. It lists B. Ramakrishna Reddy, B. P. Mahapatra and Joy Reddy as authors, with E. Annamalai as editor, and gives 2000 as the publication year. These are details of a particular collection, rather than a claim that all Kuvi storytelling follows one written form.

A tale, a song and a riddle invite different kinds of attention. When reading with someone who knows the language, ask what changes when a performance becomes a printed text: where a voice pauses, how an answer is withheld, or which words need explanation. The catalogue is a way to find the collection; it cannot replace hearing or reading the individual pieces.

sections.title: From a familiar picture to a written word

paragraphs.text: The Kuwi Primer linked by CIIL was prepared in an NCERT workshop with the Central University of Odisha, Koraput. Its credits name instructors, coordinators, resource people and a social worker, including Sibo Sankar Patnaik, Paramananda Patel and Hanak Tadingi. Making a learning book involves choosing which familiar words and experiences will help a reader begin.

On page 13, a house photograph sits beside a short passage; below are pictures of bricks, soil and a cat with paired labels. A large letter and empty writing boxes turn recognition into practice. Earlier charts separately present Kuvi letters and additional Odia letters. The layout makes the difference between learning a language and learning to write it visible on the page.

sections.title: A different kind of reading companion

paragraphs.text: The 2018 Kuvi booklet on the reading shelf arranges English, Odia and Kuvi in parallel columns. Unlike the picture lesson, it invites comparison across languages. Try following one row with a reader or teacher, then ask for a sentence in which the word is used. A column can offer a starting point without showing every setting in which a word belongs.

sections.title: Keep the book and the speaker in view

paragraphs.text: Choose one small task: look closely at a primer page, compare a booklet row, or find a tale from the named collection. Keep the title, contributor and edition with your notes. That gives a future conversation something precise to return to, and leaves room for another reader to explain a different usage.

pages.title: Saora / Sora
pages.lead: Read a picture lesson, compare a trilingual page, and follow the people and scripts behind Saora / Sora learning materials.

paragraphs.text: Saora, Sora and Savara are names recorded for a language in the South Munda group of the Austroasiatic family. A book’s spelling is a useful starting point; ask a reader which name they use.

sections.title: A page with a place behind it

paragraphs.text: CIIL locates many speakers in Gajapati, Rayagada and Ganjam. The learning books below bring that broad geography closer through named teachers, speakers and localities.

sections.title: More than one way to write

paragraphs.text: Sora has been written in Latin, Odia and Telugu letters, as well as Sorang Sompeng. Recognising a script does not, by itself, identify the language written in it.

Two institutional accounts date Sorang Sompeng to 1936 but differ over its inventor. CIIL credits Malia Gomango and describes Mangei Gomango’s role in promoting it through a letterpress. The Unicode Standard credits Mangei with devising the script. The date is shared; the attribution remains a difference between these accounts.

The 2024 Savara (Sora) Primer names Enam Gomango, a teacher at Palapur, and Sora speakers Opino Gomango of Luhangar and Lisu Gomango of Gunupur among its resource people. Published by CIIL with NCERT, it is intended for early childhood and adult literacy. The credit page shows whose knowledge helped shape this particular learning book.

On printed page 3, a large Odia letter appears alongside a short passage and labelled pictures, including a leaf, an open mouth and fruit. Below them, progressively paler letter forms lead to an empty writing box. The page moves from recognising an object to seeing a written form and practising it by hand.

sections.title: From a word column to a story

paragraphs.text: The 2018 Saora booklet offers another approach. Its English, Odia and Saora columns move from pronouns to topics such as crops, household objects and everyday sentences. Open a page with a reader and follow one row; then ask how the word would enter a conversation. The printed comparison is a starting point for use, rather than a substitute for it.

For connected reading, SCSTRTI lists three Saora volumes of Pilanka Katha. Its account of the series describes illustrated materials drawn from tales, songs and riddles for children. That is a different invitation from a word list: find a complete piece, keep its title and contributor with it, and listen to how a reader carries it from beginning to end.

pages.title: Sarala Das
pages.lead: Sarala Das’s Mahabharata asks readers to meet familiar characters again. A prayer turns towards Chandrabhaga; a plotter has to reckon with the deaths of soldiers. The epic’s language and its moral choices belong together.

sections.title: An epic with its own choices

paragraphs.text: Sarala Das belongs to the fifteenth century. Ganeswar Mishra’s literary overview places his Mahabharata in that period; B. N. Patnaik describes the poet, remembered as Adikavi, as a creative reteller. The familiar family conflict becomes a work whose characters can act and reason differently.

The poet’s life is less securely known than his literary importance. Ujaan Ghosh connects the broad dating to a royal name within the work, while emphasising the scarcity of biographical evidence. An exact birth year would imply more certainty than this evidence offers.

In the Draupadi episode examined by Ghosh, Krishna directs her appeal towards Surya. Her prayer names Chandrabhaga on the coast; the Sun sends Chaya and Maya to keep her clothed. Ghosh reads this as a redistribution of divine agency: Krishna remains involved, but another deity provides the rescue. A place in Odisha becomes part of how the crisis is answered.

Read the prayer with that change in mind. Who receives the appeal, who acts, and whose power becomes visible? Following those decisions gives a reader more to notice than whether a remembered storyline has been reproduced.

sections.title: Sakuni and the cost of revenge

paragraphs.text: Patnaik’s account gives Sakuni a responsibility beyond his revenge. Bound to avenge his father and relatives, he could eventually return to his kingdom. Instead, he chooses death on the battlefield, holding himself responsible for innocent soldiers killed in the war. Patnaik’s reading draws attention to the people whose deaths a contest between royal families can leave out of view.

The question here is not simply whether Sakuni succeeds. It is what success leaves him answerable for. A character can remain implicated in violence while also recognising its cost; that recognition changes how we read his last choice.

Patnaik also describes Sarala’s account of his own writing: he professes little learning and presents himself as the scribe of goddess Sarala’s inspiration. This is a religious account of poetic authority. It tells us how the poet wishes his words to be received; it cannot by itself establish a literal history of his education or a miraculous event.

That distinction leaves room to take devotion seriously. The claim asks a listener to hear a voice authorised by the goddess. It can be read for what it does within the work, without turning it into a dated biographical incident.

sections.title: Know which text you are reading

paragraphs.text: Copies matter. Ghosh uses Artaballabh Mohanty’s multi-volume edition, published from 1965, and explains that it draws on manuscripts with differing readings. His citations use pages rather than verse numbers. His study does not describe a single, settled critical text. An episode encountered in one edition therefore needs its edition details alongside it.

The Government of Odisha’s Sarala Mahabharata catalogue offers numbered PDF downloads, giving readers a way to approach the Odia text. A catalogue label alone does not identify its relationship to Mohanty’s edition. Keep the file, parva, page and any editor or publication details with a passage before comparing it with a scholar’s account.

Begin with one episode and stay with its choices: the destination of a prayer, the reason for a decision, the person left to bear its consequences. Read the Odia with someone who knows the language when needed. Let a remembered version start the conversation, while giving this one time to speak.

pages.title: Pratibha Ray
pages.lead: Draupadi is walking towards heaven, yet the promised destination troubles her. In Pratibha Ray’s Jajnaseni, the journey gives a woman room to question what her life has meant.

paragraphs.text: Pratibha Ray’s professional account traces a working life from school teaching to Odisha’s government colleges. She took voluntary retirement as a Professor of Education in 1998. That career belongs alongside the novels and stories: it is part of the life behind the writing, though it does not explain every choice a fictional character makes.

sections.title: Draupadi asks what the journey means

paragraphs.text: The English excerpt of Jajnaseni on Ray’s website places us inside Draupadi’s thoughts during the Himalayan ascent. She asks whether the wish to reach heaven can itself become an attachment. The contrast between iron and gold makes the question sharper: a desire may seem purer while still binding the person who holds it.

Her thoughts then turn to an unfinished life. What has she accomplished, and what remains wanting? She slips; her five husbands continue without looking back. Told from her position, their onward movement becomes an experience of abandonment. The episode asks us to attend to the person left behind.

Pause at the change from inward questioning to the fall. How does a sentence about spiritual purpose prepare us to read an action between people? Following that movement gives this short passage its force.

Ray’s account of adaptations records Hema Malini’s stage ballet of Jajnaseni. It also names an Odissi ballet drawn from Mahamoha, her novel about Ahalya. These are two examples of her fiction moving into performance; the account supplies no dates for these productions.

An inward question on the page poses a practical problem on stage. A performer may have to carry it through gesture, movement, music or speech. When comparing a book and an adaptation, choose one moment and notice what the new form makes available to its audience.

sections.title: Keep the translator and edition in view

paragraphs.text: Pradip Bhattacharya’s bibliography identifies his English translation as Yajnaseni: The Story of Draupadi, published by Rupa in 1995. Ray’s website labels its English passage Jajnaseni but does not name its translator. The credited book edition and that online excerpt should therefore be kept distinct.

The original publication year needs care too. The Library of Congress reading page lists a first Nalanda edition from 1984, while its biographical paragraph gives 1985. Until the original imprint settles that difference, retain the date attached to the particular edition rather than treating either year as an uncontested starting point.

sections.title: Read with an ear for the voice

paragraphs.text: The Library of Congress also lists audio excerpts of Ray reading from Yajnaseni and other works. Its Yajnaseni entries are labelled pages 1–3 and 447–451. Those page references offer a way to keep a listening session tied to a text, provided the edition in hand matches the listed copy.

Begin with a short passage. Mark the questions, then notice where the sentences pause and turn. Keep a note of the language, translator and edition. Leave room for the next passage to complicate the first impression.

pages.title: Bhima Bhoi
pages.lead: Whose suffering should a prayer ask to end? Begin there.

sections.title: A basket at the guru’s feet

paragraphs.text: In the English selection from Stuti Chintamani’s twenty-seventh boli, or canto, printed in Sitakant Mahapatra’s study, sins become a burden carried in a basket to the guru’s feet. The plea then widens to other devotees and finally to the suffering world. The speaker is willing to face damnation if others can be redeemed.
Read the whole selection before its final appeal. Where does the request move beyond the speaker?

The prayer belongs to Mahima Dharma. Mahapatra explains Alekha as the indescribable divine and nirakara as formless. These terms help locate the appeal within a faith, rather than treating it as a free-standing slogan.

sections.title: Find a passage you can return to

paragraphs.text: The National Book Trust’s 2026 catalogue describes Stuti Chintamani as a work of 100 cantos, each with 20 stanzas. It credits Satyananda Swain as the English translator of Gems of Soulful Prayer: Stuti Chintamani of Bhima Bhoi, published in 2024. That edition offers a longer reading route than the selections in Mahapatra’s monograph.

Keep the translator’s name with the words you read. If two English versions seem different, set one short passage beside the other and mark the choices: who is addressed, what burden is named, and whose relief is sought? A comparison becomes useful when you can point to the words that prompted it.

sections.title: A remembered life is not a settled biography

paragraphs.text: Mahapatra opens his biography with uncertainty about Bhima Bhoi’s exact birth date, birthplace and blindness. The poetry cannot settle those questions simply because its speaker describes suffering.

Johannes Beltz makes this distinction central to his study of the poet’s remembered life. During fieldwork in western Odisha in 2000–2001, he collected stories from ascetics and lay people. He reads miraculous birth stories as evidence of how people honoured Bhima Bhoi, rather than as verified accounts of his birth.

That leaves two worthwhile questions open: what can a document establish about a life, and what does a story reveal about the people who tell it? Keeping them separate lets us take a tradition seriously without converting every remembered event into a historical fact.

Beltz also describes a disagreement over the authority of Bhima Bhoi’s writings. In the Joranda dispute he examines, Kaupinadharis treated the texts as a code to follow; the Balkaladhari position he cites accepted them as religious books alongside others. This is a specific historical account, not a description of every follower’s position today. It shows why the same poetry can matter differently to different communities.

sections.title: Khaliapali and the life around the poems

paragraphs.text: Mahapatra places Bhima Bhoi’s later activities at Khaliapali and credits Ma Annapurna with supervising its ashram from 1877. Remembering her makes room for the work of sustaining a community around the poet.

The photograph here shows the Khaliapali memorial in 2012. It is a later place of remembrance, not a portrait of Bhima Bhoi or a reconstruction of his lifetime. The photographer, Pdhmishra, released the image under CC0.

If you follow this reading with a visit, ask locally about access and observances. Take one passage with you and leave room for what a custodian or fellow reader may explain. Record who offered an interpretation, rather than assuming that one answer speaks for everyone.

pages.title: Gopinath Mohanty
pages.lead: A knot in a rope can count a year of work. It cannot decide how much debt remains. In Paraja, Gopinath Mohanty makes unequal power visible through such small, ordinary things.

paragraphs.text: In a passage from Paraja reproduced in an IGNOU study unit, a goti, or debt-bound labourer, marks each completed year of service with a knot in a rope. The same study traces how a fine leads Sukru Jani to borrow from the moneylender, the Sahukar. Working for him keeps Sukru and his sons from ploughing their own land.

The rope records time faithfully, but the lender controls the terms on which time becomes repayment. Read the image beside the account of the family’s work: losing the use of one’s land is also losing the time needed to live from it.
This reading begins with selected English passages reproduced in teaching material. They give us something precise to return to; they do not stand in for the whole novel or its Odia text.

sections.title: Who speaks, and in whose language?

paragraphs.text: Another teaching unit places transliterated Odia beside the English translation. In a chapter-two encounter, the Forest Guard addresses Jili while she washes leaves for cooking. The unit points to changes between local speech, colloquial Odia and the narrator’s standard Odia. In English, the reader is told that he speaks her dialect, but cannot hear those shifts in the same way.

That is a useful question to carry into a translation: when does a voice sound different from the narrator’s, and how is that difference conveyed? A note about dialect, a retained word and a change of sentence rhythm do different kinds of work.

The unit also shows a field mouse whose lifetime of gathering can be scattered by one gust. Here, an animal’s small store gives the reader a scale for human vulnerability: the long effort of accumulation against the speed of loss.

Return to the rope and the mouse together. One measures years; the other makes destruction almost instantaneous. What happens to the familiar picture of a rural landscape when we notice labour, time and the possibility of dispossession within it?

Born in 1914 at Nagabali in Cuttack, Mohanty entered administrative service in 1938. His memorial biography places his early postings in Koraput and connects them with his interest in local languages and lives. It also records his translations of Tolstoy’s War and Peace and Gorky’s My Universities: his literary world extended beyond the landscapes for which he is often remembered.

An administrator can encounter both everyday life and the institutions that govern it. That position is worth keeping in mind as we read. A novelist’s choices of scene, voice and sympathy remain choices; fictional characters cannot speak for every member of a community today.

sections.title: Choose an edition, then keep reading

paragraphs.text: The memorial bibliography dates the Odia Paraja to 1945. An Oxford-published bibliography separately identifies the 1987 English translation by Bikram K. Das. The current Oxford product page gives 1 June 1997 for the paperback with ISBN 9780195623918. These are different records in the book’s history, not three competing dates for its first appearance.

Keep the translator, publisher and year with your reading notes; page numbers in a teaching excerpt may not match your copy. Follow one exchange beyond its quoted lines. Notice what each person wants, what they can refuse, and who has the power to make an account of events count.

pages.title: Juang
pages.lead: A house of memory. A language of its own. Follow the words into everyday life.

paragraphs.text: CIIL identifies Juang as a Munda language within the Austroasiatic family, spoken in parts of Keonjhar, Angul and Dhenkanal. Juang is the language’s name; Munda describes a wider language group.
This is a starting point, not a complete map of speakers. Community identity, home language and the language someone uses at school or work need not be the same.
CIIL also describes Juang being written in the Odia script. A shared writing system is a bridge for readers; it does not make the languages identical.

SCSTRTI describes the majang, also called mandaghar, as a community institution with roles in gatherings, music and shared resources. Its account also records an origin belief connecting ancestors to Rusi Tangar near Gonasika. This is a reported tradition, not an archaeological finding.

Begin with a story its teller wants to share. Ask how place names are pronounced, who taught the story and whether it is appropriate to publish. A public retelling should keep the teller’s context, credit and choice of words.

pages.title: Gangadhar Meher
pages.lead: A familiar epic changes when we stay with the person left behind. Gangadhar Meher’s Tapaswini invites that attention.
pages.identity_note: An editorial reading panel, not a portrait or quotation.

paragraphs.text: In Harekrishna Meher’s English rendering of Canto IV, dawn approaches Sita’s cottage as a visitor. Leaves become hands carrying dew; birds supply the greeting. A woman living in exile receives the attention of a queen. The landscape does more than surround her: it recognises her.

Sita responds with reverence, but her thoughts still turn to Rama. She asks dawn to bring him good fortune. The tenderness of this welcome does not erase her attachment or her grief. Both remain present in the same morning.

At the river, Tamasa embraces Sita with waves. She describes continuing through obstacles and giving water to those along her banks. Movement, shelter and service become ways of speaking about endurance.

Harekrishna Meher’s critical account places the poem after Sita’s banishment, at Valmiki’s hermitage, and relates it to the Ramayana, Kalidasa’s Raghuvamsha and Bhavabhuti’s Uttararamacharita. He identifies the caring hermitess Anukampa as Meher’s addition. That surrounding company matters: attention falls on how a separated woman is received and supported.

The poem also honours devotion to a husband. In the preface discussed by Harekrishna Meher, that devotion is central to Sita’s life in exile. A reader can value the care she receives while questioning the obligations she is asked to uphold.

Sambalpur district’s biography places Gangadhar Meher in a weaving family at Barpali. It lists several works, including Pranaya Ballari, Kichaka Badha and Indumati. Tapaswini is one entrance into that larger body of writing, rather than a substitute for it.

A life story can introduce a writer without explaining every line. Keep the craft connection as a question rather than a ready-made answer: where do you actually hear repetition, variation or a pattern returning? Let the language supply the evidence.

The English passages discussed here are Harekrishna Meher’s. His publication account identifies Tapasvini of Gangadhara Meher, issued by R.N. Bhattacharya in 2009. A different reading route is Gangadhar Meher: Selected Works, published by Aryan Books International in 2001 and edited by Madhusudan Pati. Its publisher credits eight translators; that collective credit does not identify who translated each individual poem.

Begin with one canto and keep the translator’s name beside your notes. If you can read Odia, compare an identified edition with the English; otherwise, notice the English version’s choices without assuming they reproduce every sound of the original. This introduction follows selected passages and a translator’s criticism, not a complete comparison of the epic and all its sources.

pages.title: Sambalpuri
pages.kicker: Western Odisha · song · a language of belonging
pages.lead: A song can reach you before a map does. Begin with its makers, then listen for the world around it.
identity_panel: A song. A voice. A place.

paragraphs.text: Sambalpur district’s cultural account describes Sambalpuri as spoken in western Odisha and distinguishes it from speech in coastal districts. Its account places language beside music, dance and festivals.
Sambalpuri and Kosali are names readers may encounter. We preserve the wording of each source rather than treating the names, their extent or their preferred use as settled for every speaker.

A January 2022 Odisha Review interview with lyricist Mitrabhanu Gountia connects “Rangabati” with composer Prabhudatta Pradhan and singers Jitendriya Haripal and Krishna Patel. The account traces the song through All India Radio, Sambalpur, and a later commercial recording.

Gountia recalls turning towards writing in his mother tongue and describes a wider literary life of lyrics, plays and prose. Read this as a writer’s account of his practice and aspirations, not a complete history of the language.
When you find an authorised recording, keep the lyricist, composer, singers and version together. A familiar refrain becomes richer when its makers remain visible.

The district account connects Nuakhai with new rice, family gatherings and greetings, and describes Dalkhai through song and dance. These are cultural connections to explore with local context, not a programme of performances available on demand.
Ask a willing reader for a poem they return to, or a host about a greeting used in their own family. Leave space for an answer that differs from the printed description.

pages.title: Desia
pages.lead: A language belongs on a stage and in a child’s first book. Follow two documented moments in Desia’s continuing story.
identity_panel: Listen to the people behind the name

paragraphs.text: The Census entry Desia gives this introduction a statistical starting point. It does not make every related name interchangeable. SCSTRTI’s learning catalogue also uses Bhatri-Desia; the relationship between these labels needs speaker and specialist context.
Our population panel uses only the entry explicitly labelled Desia. It does not absorb Bhatri, infer ancestry or draw a boundary around every person who uses Desia.

On 2 June 2023, the Ministry of Education reported a workshop involving NCERT’s Regional Institute of Education, Bhubaneswar, and the Central University of Odisha. Participants prepared learning materials in Kui and Desia, with listening, speaking, reading and writing in view. The release described testing and revision still to come.

The moment matters: a language familiar at home was being considered for the first steps of classroom learning. The report is evidence of that work in 2023, not a guarantee that a particular book is available today.

SCSTRTI’s January–June 2024 newsletter reports multilingual dramas in Santali, Mundari, Desia and Ho at Adivasi Mela 2024 in Bhubaneswar. The same newsletter lists school learning publications spanning Desia, Koya, Sadri and Ho.

A classroom and a stage offer two doors into this story. With a willing teacher, reader or performer, ask what they read, how they name their language and which stories they want to carry forward. A fuller history of Desia literature and oral traditions needs named works, tellers and versions.
